summary: Describes server-based sorting and threading extensions for IMAP. They let the server do the sorting and grouping into conversations, which can greatly improve performance for clients showing sorted or threaded views. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Rather than the email program sorting thousands of messages itself, it asks the server to line them up and group replies.

subtitle: Let the IMAP server sort a mailbox and group replies into conversations, so the client does not have to download everything first.

tldr.problem: Mail clients that show sorted or threaded views normally have to download the data for every message and do the work themselves.
tldr.mechanism: The SORT and THREAD commands extend IMAP so the server searches, sorts and groups messages and returns just a list of message numbers. THREAD offers two algorithms, ORDEREDSUBJECT and REFERENCES.
tldr.outcome: Clients get sorted and threaded views with far less data transfer. RFC 5256 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 5957.

facts.label: Sort keys
facts.value: ARRIVAL, CC, DATE, FROM, SIZE, SUBJECT, TO

facts.label: Capability names
facts.value: SORT, and THREAD= plus an algorithm name

today: RFC 5256 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2008 and has been updated by RFC 5957. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Sort and Thread on the Server
sections.content:
RFC 5256 adds two extensions to IMAP: SORT and THREAD. They provide server-based sorting and threading of messages, without requiring the client to download the data needed to do it itself. The abstract says this gives substantial performance improvements for clients that offer sorted and threaded views.

A server announces base-level sorting with a capability name that starts with SORT. It announces threading with one or more capability names of the form THREAD= followed by an algorithm name. Future upwards-compatible extensions are meant to build on these names.

Servers that implement either extension MUST collate strings according to the rules of I18NLEVEL=1 from RFC 5255, and SHOULD advertise that extension.
sections.eli5: Your email program can ask the server, 'please line these messages up for me.' The server does the heavy lifting so your program does not have to carry every message home first.

sections.title: Base Subject and Sent Date
sections.content:
Both sorting and threading rely on two normalized values. The base subject is the subject with artifacts removed, such as Re: and Fwd: prefixes, (fwd) trailers and bracketed tags. The RFC gives a seven-step procedure for it, and says all servers and disconnected clients MUST follow exactly this algorithm so a user does not get different results online and offline.

The sent date comes from the Date: header, adjusted by its time zone to UTC. If the time zone is invalid, the value SHOULD be treated as UTC. If there is no usable date, the message's INTERNALDATE is used instead. When two sent dates match exactly, the order of the messages in the mailbox (their sequence number) breaks the tie.

This differs from the date criteria of the IMAP SEARCH command, which use only the date and are not adjusted by time zone.
sections.eli5: Before sorting by title, the server first scrapes off the 'Re:' and 'Fwd:' stickers so 'Re: Pizza' and 'Pizza' count as the same thing. For dates it converts everyone's clock to one shared clock.

sections.title: The SORT Command
sections.content:
SORT is a variant of SEARCH with sorting semantics. It takes a parenthesized list of sort criteria, a mandatory charset, and one or more searching criteria. The server finds the matching messages and returns them in an untagged SORT response. UID SORT does the same but returns unique identifiers instead of sequence numbers. The US-ASCII and UTF-8 charsets MUST be implemented.

The sort keys are ARRIVAL, CC, DATE, FROM, SIZE, SUBJECT and TO. Sorting is ascending, and the modifier REVERSE flips a single following criterion. With several criteria, they apply in priority order, so (SUBJECT DATE) sorts by base subject and then by sent date within equal subjects. Messages that tie on every criterion keep mailbox order, as if there were an implicit sequence-number criterion.

REVERSE does not affect that implicit sequence-number tie-break, so REVERSE SUBJECT is not the same as reversing a SUBJECT sort. The RFC says it is generally better, and faster, to reverse the results in the client.

Untagged EXPUNGE responses are not permitted while the server is answering SORT, but are permitted during UID SORT.
sections.eli5: You tell the server how to order things, like 'by sender, then by date,' and it hands back a list of message numbers in that order. If two messages look identical to the sorter, the older spot in the mailbox goes first.

sections.title: The THREAD Command and Its Algorithms
sections.content:
THREAD takes a threading algorithm, a charset and searching criteria, and returns an untagged THREAD response. Two algorithms are defined.

ORDEREDSUBJECT, nicknamed 'poor man's threading', sorts the matched messages by base subject and then sent date, splits them into threads that share a base subject, and orders the threads by the sent date of their first message. The result is shallow: the first message of each thread is at the root, and every later message is a child of that first one, so there are no grandchildren.

REFERENCES groups messages by who replied to whom. It rebuilds each message's ancestry from the References header, falling back to the first valid Message ID in In-Reply-To. It also checks the original subject to see whether a message is a reply or forward. The algorithm has six main steps: link messages by their references (creating dummy messages for missing IDs and never creating a link that would form a loop), gather parentless messages under a root, prune dummies, sort top-level siblings by sent date, merge threads that share a base subject, and finally sort each set of siblings by sent date.

Message IDs MUST be normalized before comparison, so that a quoted and an unquoted form of the same ID match. Message ID comparisons are case-sensitive, while subject comparisons are case-insensitive.
sections.eli5: One way to group emails is simply 'same title goes together.' The smarter way follows the chain of who answered whom, like tracing a family tree, and then tidies up leftovers with the same title.

sections.title: SORT and THREAD Responses
sections.content:
The SORT response is simply zero or more numbers separated by spaces: sequence numbers for SORT, unique identifiers for UID SORT.

The THREAD response carries zero or more threads, each a parenthesized list of members. Numbers within a list are successive parent and child. When a thread splits, it nests into sub-threads whose first members are siblings, and there is no limit to the nesting. So the response THREAD (2)(3 6 (4 23)(44 7 96)) holds message 2 alone, and a second thread where 3 is the parent of 6, and 6 has two branches: 4 then 23, and 44 then 7 then 96.

In the response THREAD ((3)(5)), messages 3 and 5 are siblings of a parent that does not match the search or does not exist in the mailbox, yet they belong to the same thread.
sections.eli5: The answer is a list of numbers. Brackets show who belongs together: numbers in a row are a parent, then its child, then its child, and a new bracket means the conversation branched.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The RFC defines the grammar in ABNF. A sort command is ["UID" SP] "SORT" SP sort-criteria SP search-criteria, where each criterion is an optional REVERSE and a sort key. A thread command names an algorithm that is ORDEREDSUBJECT, REFERENCES or an extension algorithm, and extension algorithms MUST be registered with IANA.

The same section gives rules for base subject extraction, including subj-refwd (re or fw/fwd), subj-blob (text in square brackets), subj-fwd-hdr ([fwd:) and the trailer (fwd).
sections.eli5: This part is the exact spelling book for the commands, so every mail program writes and reads them the same way.

sections.title: Security, Internationalization and Registration
sections.content:
The extensions raise no security considerations beyond those of base IMAP. The RFC reminds readers that IMAP traffic is sent in the clear unless protection such as STARTTLS or privacy protection in AUTHENTICATE is negotiated. It also warns that sorting by REFERENCES can produce misleading thread trees, for example when a message carries false References data and pulls a thread into another one. Base subject extraction can mis-collate if the removed text was real content rather than a subject artifact.

For internationalization, strings are collated with the i;unicode-casemap collation. Translated forms of re and fw are deliberately not handled; the RFC suggests using re: and a standard forward token in messages and localizing them at display time.

IANA registration: the document registers the SORT and THREAD capabilities and creates a new IMAP threading algorithms registry containing ORDEREDSUBJECT and REFERENCES.
sections.eli5: Sorting does not add new dangers, but messages can still lie about whom they answer, and that can fool the grouping. Like everything in IMAP, it is only private if the connection is protected.

C: A282 SORT (SUBJECT) UTF-8 SINCE 1-Feb-1994
S: * SORT 2 84 882
S: A282 OK SORT completed
C: A283 SORT (SUBJECT REVERSE DATE) UTF-8 ALL
S: * SORT 5 3 4 1 2
S: A283 OK SORT completed
